query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a modest (approximately 5 at.%) Hf addition into nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will alter the local chemical ordering so as to suppress the radiation‐induced Cr–V precipitate formation while retaining the alloy’s inherently low irradiation hardening and enhancing its bulk processing feasibility.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline quaternary W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced via magnetron sputtering with a bimodal grain size distribution (majority <100 nm) and exhibiting ~3–5 nm Cr–V precipitates after irradiation
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with approximately 5 atomic percent Hf
generation.conditions: Irradiation with energetic particles (e.g., 3 MeV ions) to accumulate around 8 dpa at elevated temperatures near 1073 K, which are representative of fusion service conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of short-range ordering (SRO) in the Cr–V sublattice by Hf, leading to a more homogenized chemical distribution and stabilization of the nanocrystalline BCC structure
generation.mechanism: Hf atoms perturb the local chemical environment, reducing the thermodynamic driving force for Cr–V segregation and subsequent nano-precipitate nucleation. This intervention leverages the evidence that Hf addition in a similar W-Ta-Cr-V system leads to element homogenization and suppression of Cr–V precipitation, while maintaining a high hardness level and thermal stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy, the Hf-modified alloy is expected to exhibit a significant reduction (to near-undetectable levels) of Cr–V precipitate density, maintain negligible irradiation hardening as measured by nanoindentation (i.e. hardness change remains minimal), and show improved microstructural homogeneity that is more amenable to bulk fabrication processes.
generation.baseline: The unmodified alloy shows ~3–5 nm Cr–V precipitates (density ~0.03 nm⁻²) emerging under similar irradiation conditions with only slight irradiation hardening, but with challenges in scaling the thin-film deposition process to bulk production.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for irradiation conditions up to ~8 dpa and temperatures on the order of 1073 K. It is targeted at the regime relevant to fusion reactor service and assumes processing parameters that can be translated from thin-film deposition to bulk powder metallurgy or sintering routes.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (PMC10154406::web::015::high_thermal_stability and PMC6397024::web::017::conclusions) support the beneficial effect of Hf on suppressing Cr–V precipitation, the optimal Hf concentration for nanocrystalline structures and scalability to bulk fabrication remains uncertain and is being explored in this study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: the baseline nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy and an Hf-modified variant with ~5 at.% Hf, using identical processing techniques. Subject both sets to energetic particle irradiation (e.g., 3 MeV ions) to a dose of approximately 8 dpa at 1073 K. Characterize the irradiated microstructures using TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify the size, density, and distribution of any precipitates. Assess mechanical properties via nanoindentation to evaluate irradiation-induced hardening. Ensure the bulk processing viability is also tested through sintering experiments.
measurements: TEM imaging and APT analysis for precipitate presence, size (expectation: lack or significant reduction of 3–5 nm Cr–V precipitates in the Hf-modified alloy)
Nanoindentation hardness measurements (expectation: similar or negligible increase in hardness compared to the unmodified alloy)
Density and grain size analysis post-sintering for bulk fabrication relevance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-modified alloy exhibits a precipitate density and size comparable to or exceeding that of the unmodified alloy, or if it shows a significant increase in irradiation hardening (indicating adverse changes in mechanical properties), or if the processing for bulk fabrication is adversely affected, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles.
